header:
hypotheses.yaml — Key Personnel · the legacy hypothesis ledger
The author supplied a private 60-row staffing trade-off matrix in eight categories (2026-10-21) and said, in his words,
that the rows "are just my best guesses" and that this "applies to their categories as well". Every row and every category
is therefore carried here as a HYPOTHESIS, never as a source of fact. The sweeps test each against the corpus; the app
renders the ledger on /methods. Firm-specific wording has been removed; "the company" means any customer-governed small firm.

status: untested | supported | partly-supported | contradicted | unstudied | reframed
  supported         the corpus contains evidence for the mechanism and the mitigation as stated (cite it in evidence)
  partly-supported  mechanism supported, mitigation or trade-off qualified or narrowed (say how)
  contradicted      the corpus says otherwise (cite it)
  unstudied         searched; no evidence either way (log the queries)
  reframed          the category or row dissolves into other records (list them in mapped_to)
mapped_to: the constraint, lever, gate or stage ids that absorb the hypothesis once the records exist
evidence: one or two cited sentences [n]; empty until adjudicated

entries.evidence: The category becomes the attract stage; its rows map onto evidence-derived constraints (local pool, posting, channel mix, referral network, employer image, ad wording, credential requirements, cleared supply). The recruitment literature organises itself by source, attraction predictors and posting economics [62](#cite:62) [63](#cite:63) [65](#cite:65).

The category becomes the definition half of the plan stage. Its rows reduce to three sources of requirement that have to be reconciled before a posting, the contract's labor category [99](#cite:99), the selection evidence's scored criteria [1](#cite:1) [7](#cite:7), and the customer's standard, bounded by the personal-services rule [197](#cite:197), plus the clock the customer's review runs on [188](#cite:188) [15](#cite:15). B3 (eligibility) was adjudicated in sweep 1 and B4 (immediate productivity) lands in the onboard stage.

entries.original: Clearance access and readiness to start
entries.evidence: The category becomes the clear-and-start stage. Its six rows map onto seven constraints: C1 sponsorship, C2 the clearance clock, C3 eligibility against access, C4 the interval, C5 unbillable payroll, C6 the start-date clocks and the access checklist; the evidence adds a seventh the matrix lacked, the foreign-national hire [132](#cite:132) [131](#cite:131). The rules organise the stage better than the rows did: who may request (32 CFR 117.10), who sponsors the facility (117.9), what transfers (SEAD 7), what an interim reaches (117.10(l)), what a credential needs (32 CFR 157, 161.7) [119](#cite:119) [120](#cite:120) [122](#cite:122) [137](#cite:137) [138](#cite:138).

The category splits: D1-D4 are offer-stage constraints (the rate ceiling, the lagging rate, the total-compensation comparison, compression of incumbents); D5-D7 (acquisition budget, cash, vacancy cost) are plan-stage economics adjudicated in sweep 7. The literature organises itself by contract cost principles, personnel economics and the transparency evidence [98](#cite:98) [91](#cite:91) [93](#cite:93).

The category dissolves into the lifecycle stages: E2, E3, E4 and E6 are select-stage constraints and levers; E7 belongs to the offer stage; E1 and E8 are plan-stage (ownership and records) and are adjudicated in sweep 7. The selection literature organises itself by predictor validity, applicant reactions and decision method rather than by "execution" [26](#cite:26) [27](#cite:27).

The category splits into two stages. Onboarding, which the matrix had no category for, carries the adjustment evidence [152](#cite:152) [155](#cite:155) [156](#cite:156) and the ramp [157](#cite:157); develop carries the training economics [159](#cite:159) [161](#cite:161) [160](#cite:160), the transfer conditions [162](#cite:162), mentoring [158](#cite:158) [164](#cite:164) [165](#cite:165) and the legal and cost rules on holding the investment [166](#cite:166) [167](#cite:167) [168](#cite:168) [175](#cite:175) [174](#cite:174). The eight rows map onto eight constraints, with F7 and F8 merging into the unmeasured return and the unplaced development.

The category becomes the retain stage, organised by the ranked turnover predictors [178](#cite:178) rather than by the employee experience: G1 pay (comparison), G2 steps up, G3 and G4 merge into the firm's absence and the customer-run work, G5 the strain of covering a vacancy, G6 the arrangements the job cannot offer, G7 the contract's end, G8 the external premium and the law on restrictions. The rows said what the predictors say; the predictors say which of them matters most, and pay is not first.

The category becomes the economics and planning half of the plan stage: whether the opening is real [119](#cite:119) [203](#cite:203), whether anyone forecast it [205](#cite:205), whether the role can be staffed under the rate [206](#cite:206) [98](#cite:98), how far partners can fill it [198](#cite:198) [199](#cite:199), and whether the firm reasons from records or anecdote [204](#cite:204) [200](#cite:200). H4 and H5 were adjudicated in the handover stage.

original.challenge: Too few qualified candidates locally
original.mitigation: Expand geographic sourcing; test relocation interest early; seek approved flexibility.
original.tradeoff: Relocation costs and longer lead time; onsite requirements may remain binding.
original.dependencies: Requires affordable offers (D1), relocation budget (D5), and workable schedules (G6).

entries.evidence: Local scarcity is documented: 87% of small businesses hiring report few or no qualified applicants [71](#cite:71). Geographic expansion by relocation is weakly supported as a remedy because relocation has fallen to 1.6% of job seekers [85](#cite:85); the evidence-based reach lever is remote or hybrid work, which workers value at 8% of pay [70](#cite:70), and that is unavailable for onsite or cleared roles, as the row said. "Test relocation interest early" is untested as a practice.
queries: NFIB September 2026 jobs report
Challenger relocation Q1 2023
Barrero Bloom Davis WFH valuation

original.challenge: Rare mix of skills, domain knowledge, and clearance
original.mitigation: Separate essential entry requirements from learnable skills; target adjacent experience.
original.tradeoff: Larger pool requires training and customer acceptance of a learning curve.
original.dependencies: Requires requirement flexibility (B2), customer alignment (B5), and a training path (F1).

entries.evidence: The cleared half is supported: no individual can initiate a clearance and the contractor-held pool is finite [80](#cite:80), and the pay premium by level is documented [89](#cite:89). Separating essential from learnable requirements is supported by the validity evidence (experience-years .07) [1](#cite:1) and by the skills-based-hiring findings [68](#cite:68). The training-path half waits on sweep 5.
queries: CRS R43216 sponsorship
ClearanceJobs compensation 2025

original.challenge: Strong candidates are not actively searching
original.mitigation: Build ongoing relationships through technical networks, referrals, and targeted outreach.
original.tradeoff: Sustained effort; results may arrive too late for an immediate vacancy.
original.dependencies: Requires recruiter ownership (E1), candidate records (E8), and demand forecasts (H1).

entries.evidence: People not actively searching are reached through networks: referred applicants are more likely to be interviewed and hired and referred workers quit 10-30% less [60](#cite:60) [61](#cite:61). The trade-off (sustained effort; results arrive late) is a synthesis; the dependency on candidate records and forecasts (E8, H1) waits on sweep 7.
queries: Burks Cowgill Hoffman Housman referrals
Brown Setren Topa referrals

original.challenge: Limited visibility as an employer
original.mitigation: Use specific role descriptions, employee perspectives, and approved examples of meaningful work.
original.tradeoff: Content takes effort; visibility cannot compensate for an unattractive offer.
original.dependencies: Depends on credible total value (D3), accurate duties (B1), and employee experience (G4).

entries.evidence: Employer image affects attraction and forms through recruiters and word of mouth [64](#cite:64); job and organisation characteristics, recruiter behaviour and process perceptions predict attraction while recruiter demographics do not [63](#cite:63). "Visibility cannot compensate for an unattractive offer" is consistent with those predictors. The specific content tactics (employee perspectives, examples of work) are untested as such.
queries: Lievens Slaughter 2016 employer image
Chapman 2005 applicant attraction

original.challenge: Repeated reliance on the same channels
original.mitigation: Test a few distinct channels; track qualified candidates, starts, and retention by source.
original.tradeoff: Experiments consume budget; small samples can mislead.
original.dependencies: Requires stage data (H8) and consistent screening (E3) before comparing channels.

entries.evidence: Sources differ in tenure and performance (inside sources outperform) [62](#cite:62), so tracking by source is warranted; contractors were required to keep online search and applicant records until the Internet Applicant rule was removed effective 2026-10-26 [87](#cite:87) [86](#cite:86). The claims that experiments consume budget and small samples mislead are synthesis.
queries: Zottoli Wanous 2000 recruitment sources
OFCCP Internet Applicant rule status 2026

original.challenge: Paid postings yield volume but few suitable applicants
original.mitigation: Improve targeting and disclose critical constraints; expand spend only where qualified yield improves.
original.tradeoff: Narrow targeting reduces volume and may miss transferable skills.
original.dependencies: Clarify requirements (B2), salary (D1), and early expectations (E6) first.

entries.evidence: What a posting draws is governed by its title and pay figure (within a title, 10% higher wage draws 7.7% more applicants) [65](#cite:65); wording lowers womens appeal [77](#cite:77) and some words are unlawful [78](#cite:78); disclosing constraints early is the realistic-job-preview evidence [12](#cite:12). "Expand spend only where qualified yield improves" is synthesis.
queries: Marinescu Wolthoff power of words
Gaucher 2011 gendered wording

original.challenge: Recruiting services are expensive
original.mitigation: Reserve specialist recruiters for selected difficult or urgent roles; compare fees with vacancy costs.
original.tradeoff: Fees buy access, not guaranteed customer acceptance or retention.
original.dependencies: Requires acquisition budget (D5), vacancy economics (D7), and vacancy priority (H3).

entries.evidence: No primary source on recruiting-agency fee levels was found; the figures in circulation are vendor-stated and are not carried. What the pack carries is the benchmark the fee sits inside, median cost-per-hire \$1,200 nonexecutive and \$10,625 executive with agency fees among the components [196](#cite:196), and the vacancy-cost comparison the row's mitigation asks for [180](#cite:180) [181](#cite:181). The mitigation, reserve search for selected roles and compare fees with vacancy costs, is the lever; its effectiveness is unstudied. The trade-off, that fees buy access and not acceptance or retention, is consistent with the customer-approval and retention records.
queries: contingency recruiting agency fee percent of first-year salary survey (vendor pages only)

original.challenge: Referral networks are too narrow
original.mitigation: Add university, veteran, professional, and adjacent-industry outreach.
original.tradeoff: Broader sourcing adds relationship and evaluation work.
original.dependencies: Requires transferable-skill assessment (E3) and development capacity (F2) where needed.

entries.evidence: Referral networks are segregated and reproduce the founders composition [81](#cite:81); university and veteran pipelines are sized and governed (8.3 million veterans in the labour force [72](#cite:72); SkillBridge MOU terms [74](#cite:74); +5.6% planned graduate hiring [79](#cite:79)). "Broader sourcing adds evaluation work" is consistent with the select-stage evidence (k-009) but is a synthesis.
queries: Miller Schmutte referral hiring racial inequality
SkillBridge MOU August 2024
NACE Job Outlook 2026

original.challenge: Job description combines several jobs
original.mitigation: Identify actual deliverables and highest-priority competencies with the customer.
original.tradeoff: May require splitting work and coordinating multiple people.
original.dependencies: Requires work-model approval (H7) and viable labor economics (D1).

entries.evidence: The mechanism is supported by the posting evidence: the title and the pay figure set who applies and titles draw different pools [65](#cite:65); a labor category carries one qualification line and pays only hours by people who meet it [98](#cite:98) [99](#cite:99); a requirement must be job-related where it has adverse impact [30](#cite:30) [32](#cite:32). The mitigation, identify the deliverables and the highest-priority competencies with the customer, is the job-analysis step the selection rules assume [32](#cite:32) and is unstudied as a practice; the trade-off, splitting work across people, follows from the category rule. Dependencies on H7 and D1 are links (k-133).
queries: Marinescu Wolthoff job titles applicants; FAR 52.232-7 qualifications

original.challenge: Preferences become mandatory requirements
original.mitigation: Label requirements as contractual, customer-required, or preferred; identify approval authority.
original.tradeoff: Some constraints are binding; clarification takes customer time.
original.dependencies: Enables broader sourcing (A2); must resolve labor-category eligibility (B3).

entries.evidence: Degree lines shrink pools and dropping them in name changed hiring by almost nothing because screens did not change [68](#cite:68) [58](#cite:58); a requirement with adverse impact must be job-related and consistent with business necessity [30](#cite:30) [32](#cite:32); the customer may specify the result and reject the product but may not run the firm's hiring [197](#cite:197), so only the contract's category line is enforceable as written [99](#cite:99). The mitigation, label requirements as contractual, customer-required or preferred and identify the approval authority, is the rules' own distinction; the trade-off, that some constraints are binding and clarification takes customer time, follows. The links to A2 and B3 are drawn (k-123; B3 adjudicated in sweep 1).
queries: FAR 37.104 personal services; AEI Burning Glass skills-based hiring

original.challenge: Degree or experience thresholds exclude capable people
original.mitigation: Explore permitted equivalencies or alternative labor categories before sourcing.
original.tradeoff: Technical competence alone may not establish contractual eligibility.
original.dependencies: Requires requirement authority (B2) and rate feasibility (D1); enables skills-based review (E3).

entries.evidence: Degree and experience thresholds exclude capable people: years of job experience predicts at .07 and years of education was excluded for insufficient data in the 2022 re-estimation [1](#cite:1); exact-match filters reject qualified candidates [44](#cite:44); announced degree-requirement removals changed hiring little [58](#cite:58). The contractual-eligibility half (labor categories, equivalencies, rate feasibility) is untested until sweep 7.
queries: Sackett 2022 years of experience validity
Burning Glass skills-based hiring 2024

original.challenge: Customer expects immediate productivity
original.mitigation: Define a realistic ramp plan and useful tasks during the learning period.
original.tradeoff: Customer must accept learning time; the company may absorb mentoring cost.
original.dependencies: Requires mentoring capacity (F2), representative training (F3), and ready access (C6).

entries.evidence: The challenge is supported: the labor-category rate assumes qualified productive hours from the first day [98](#cite:98), output in the one measured ramp rose 53 percent over the first year [157](#cite:157), and a customer's reviewer applies the category line [173](#cite:173). The mitigation, a realistic ramp plan and useful tasks during the learning period, is the readiness-milestones lever (sweep 5), consistent with the transfer evidence and unstudied as a practice; the trade-off, that the customer must accept learning time and the firm absorbs mentoring cost, is the senior-hours cost (k-114). Dependencies on F2, F3 and C6 are adjudicated.

original.challenge: Company and customer define "qualified" differently
original.mitigation: Agree on a short scorecard; review an example candidate profile together.
original.tradeoff: Upfront coordination takes time but reduces rejected submissions.
original.dependencies: Depends on clear duties (B1) and essential requirements (B2); guides evaluation (E3).

entries.evidence: Three definitions of qualified coexist: the labor category's line, which the audit found unvalidated for 1,219 of 1,287 employees and breached for 101 of 112 [173](#cite:173) [99](#cite:99); the evidence's structured, scored criteria [1](#cite:1) [7](#cite:7); and the customer's reviewer's standard, which the personal-services rule allows to specify the result but not supervise the hire [197](#cite:197). The challenge is supported by that structure. The mitigation, agree a short scorecard and review an example profile together, is consistent with the structured-criteria evidence and unstudied with customers; the trade-off, upfront coordination time, follows. Dependencies on B1 and B2 are adjudicated here and E3 in sweep 1.
queries: DoD IG OASIS labor category résumé validation; Sackett 2022; Kuncel 2013

original.challenge: Rejections lack actionable feedback
original.mitigation: Request specific rejection reasons tied to agreed requirements.
original.tradeoff: Depends on customer cooperation; unexplained preferences may persist.
original.dependencies: Requires shared scorecard (B5) and recorded rejection reasons (H8).

entries.evidence: No study of customer rejection feedback, or of requesting rejection reasons, was found. The record carries the structure the row describes (three definitions of qualified; the customer's standard bounded by the personal-services rule [197](#cite:197)) and the mitigation, request specific reasons tied to agreed requirements, as a scorecard step without evidence of effect; the trade-off, dependence on customer cooperation, is the condition.
queries: customer rejection feedback contractor candidates (no evidence surfaced)

original.challenge: Requirements change during the search
original.mitigation: Reconfirm scope, compensation, and urgency whenever requirements change.
original.tradeoff: Restarting parts of the search can lose engaged candidates.
original.dependencies: Revisit pay range (D1), candidate expectations (E6), and opening credibility (H2).

entries.evidence: The consequence the row names is supported: candidates who withdraw differ in how they perceived the organisation and the process [16](#cite:16) and earlier offers are accepted more often [15](#cite:15), so a restart loses engaged candidates. The mitigation, reconfirm scope, compensation and urgency whenever requirements change, is written into the scorecard lever as a step and is unstudied; the dependencies on D1, E6 and H2 are adjudicated (E6 in sweep 2).
queries: Ryan 2000 withdrawal; Becker 2010 offer timing

original.challenge: Existing-clearance requirement narrows the pool
original.mitigation: Verify whether an already-cleared hire is essential or an authorized sponsorship path is feasible.
original.tradeoff: Sponsorship adds uncertainty and may not fit the required start date.
original.dependencies: Requires legitimate contract need, security-officer review, customer acceptance (B2), and funding (D6).

entries.evidence: The mechanism is regulation: eligibility may be requested only where access is essential to a classified contract, for the minimum number of employees, never to build a cache [119](#cite:119), and only by a firm whose facility clearance a contracting activity or cleared prime sponsored [120](#cite:120) [146](#cite:146); the already-cleared pool was about 1.35 million contractor and other personnel on the last count [80](#cite:80). The mitigation, verify whether an already-cleared hire is essential or a sponsorship path is feasible, is the lever the rules themselves imply [119](#cite:119) [146](#cite:146). The trade-off, that sponsorship adds uncertainty and may miss the start date, is supported by the 197-to-243-day industry clock [126](#cite:126) and the 45-day start rule after a pre-employment grant [119](#cite:119). The dependencies on B2 and D6 are plan-stage and untested here.
queries: 32 CFR 117.10 sponsorship need interim; 32 CFR 117.9 FCL sponsorship; DCSA FCL roadmap

original.challenge: Clearance timing misses vacancy timing
original.mitigation: Separate immediately available hiring from developmental hiring plans.
original.tradeoff: Earlier planning and potentially overlapping recruiting costs.
original.dependencies: Requires forecasts (H1), candidate timing alignment (E6), and bridge capacity (C5).

entries.evidence: Industry cases averaged 197 days for a Secret and 243 for a Top Secret end to end in FY2026 Q3 [126](#cite:126) against a 45-day median time to fill [43](#cite:43) and government targets of 40 and 75 days [54](#cite:54); the inventory rose again [54](#cite:54) and GAO found the published figures understated for five years [56](#cite:56). The mitigation, separate immediately available hiring from developmental hiring, is supported by the gap between reciprocity's five-business-day standard [122](#cite:122) and the investigation clock [126](#cite:126); the trade-off, earlier planning and overlapping recruiting costs, follows from running two tracks (synthesis). The dependency on bridge capacity (C5) and on forecasts (H1) is recorded as links; H1 waits for sweep 7.
queries: DCSA processing times 2026; NISPPAC slides Sept 2026; TW2.0 QPR FY26 Q3

original.challenge: Eligibility does not equal program or site access
original.mitigation: Have security staff identify the actual program and site access steps early.
original.tradeoff: Access dependencies may remain outside the company's control.
original.dependencies: Requires customer onboarding owners (C6) and realistic start commitments (E6).

entries.evidence: Eligibility and access are separate decisions by separate owners: a CAC needs a government sponsor, a favourable fingerprint check and a submitted investigation [138](#cite:138) [137](#cite:137); a transferred clearance a reciprocity decision due in five business days that agencies do not reliably track [122](#cite:122) [145](#cite:145); SCI and SAP on a temporary basis the granting authority's decision [119](#cite:119); a polygraph scheduled after the preliminary determination [122](#cite:122); a cyber role its certificate on commencement [139](#cite:139); at DHS the favourable-to-onboard interval ran 41 days [125](#cite:125). The mitigation, have security staff identify the actual program and site access steps early, is the checklist lever; the trade-off, that access dependencies remain outside the company's control, is exactly what GAO found for reciprocity [145](#cite:145).

original.challenge: Candidate cannot afford an uncertain start
original.mitigation: Explain milestones; explore legitimate paid bridge work with a defined budget.
original.tradeoff: The company bears nonbillable payroll exposure if the start slips.
original.dependencies: Requires useful bridge work (C5), cash capacity (D6), and credible demand (H2).

entries.evidence: The mechanism is supported by the one field study found: among 157,154 accepted offers each additional week between acceptance and start raised the odds of a no-show by 22 percent, financial security lowered them (OR 0.86), and those who left mostly took another job (39%) or cited pay (29%) [144](#cite:144). The mitigation is supported in part: company communication quality roughly halved the odds (OR 0.56) and the study recommends a named contact and milestone updates [144](#cite:144); paid bridge work has no study behind it, and its cost is the firm's indirect cost [148](#cite:148). The trade-off, nonbillable payroll exposure if the start slips, is supported by the contract and cost rules [98](#cite:98) [148](#cite:148). The population studied is entry-level and customer-facing [144](#cite:144).
queries: reneging accepted job offers start date delay study; Speer 2026 new hire ghosting HRMJ

original.challenge: No suitable work while waiting for readiness
original.mitigation: Identify approved internal or unclassified work before hiring ahead.
original.tradeoff: Useful work may be limited; internal work cannot simply be charged to the customer.
original.dependencies: Requires funded capacity (D6), bounded training (F1), and credible placement (F6).

entries.evidence: The constraint is a cost-accounting fact: a T&M contract pays only qualified hours performed on the contract [98](#cite:98) [99](#cite:99) and labor not charged to a contract is an indirect cost pooled across the firm's work [148](#cite:148), so the wait cannot be charged to the customer, as the row says. Whether unclassified contract work is open to an uncleared hire depends on the contract's security terms [146](#cite:146) (synthesis), and the firm may not sponsor ahead of a need to shorten the wait [119](#cite:119). The mitigation, identify approved internal or unclassified work before hiring ahead, is consistent with the rules but has no effectiveness evidence; the trade-off, that useful work may be limited, is unstudied. Dependencies on D6, F1 and F6 wait for sweeps 5 to 7.
queries: FAR 31.203 indirect costs; FAR 52.232-7; 32 CFR 117.10(a)(5)

original.challenge: Badging, accounts, equipment or workspace delay productivity
original.mitigation: Use a pre-start checklist with named customer and company owners.
original.tradeoff: Depends on customer responsiveness; an accepted offer is not a productive start.
original.dependencies: Requires one vacancy owner (E1), verified access steps (C3), and customer milestones (E5).

entries.evidence: Badging and accounts are governed: a CAC needs a sponsor, a favourable fingerprint check and a submitted investigation, is interim until the full investigation, and does not transfer between sponsors [138](#cite:138) [137](#cite:137); a cyber role needs its foundational certificate on commencement [139](#cite:139); the first three days carry the I-9, E-Verify and FCRA clocks [130](#cite:130) [128](#cite:128) [136](#cite:136); at one agency the interval from a favourable determination to onboarding was 41 days [125](#cite:125). The mitigation, a pre-start checklist with named customer and company owners, matches the named-contact and first-day-plan practices the no-show study recommends [144](#cite:144), but no study of checklists in this setting was found. The trade-off, dependence on customer responsiveness, is supported by GAO's reciprocity findings [145](#cite:145). Dependencies on E1 and E5 wait for sweep 7.
queries: CAC contractor eligibility TASS fingerprint; DoDM 8140.03; FAR 52.222-54; USCIS M-274; FTC consumer reports employers

original.challenge: Salary expectations exceed position economics
original.mitigation: Set a sustainable compensation range before recruiting; seek justified rate or role changes.
original.tradeoff: A technically fillable role may still be economically unattractive.
original.dependencies: Requires current rate assessment (D2), internal equity review (D4), and scope options (H7).

entries.evidence: The labor-category rate contains wages, indirect costs and profit and pays only for qualified labor [98](#cite:98) [99](#cite:99), so a salary above what the rate carries is unrecoverable; setting the range before recruiting is supported by the offer-speed evidence [15](#cite:15); "seek justified rate or role changes" maps to the adjustment clause [117](#cite:117) and to work-model changes (sweep 7). The trade-off as stated (technically fillable but economically unattractive) follows directly.
queries: FAR 16.601 T&M labor category rates
FAR 52.232-7 qualifications

original.challenge: Contract rates lag the labor market
original.mitigation: Use recruiting and retention evidence in rate discussions and future pricing.
original.tradeoff: Relief may be unavailable or too slow for the current vacancy.
original.dependencies: Requires loss reasons (H8), vacancy impact (D7), and customer engagement (B2).

entries.evidence: Market wages rose 3.1% in the year to June 2026 [103](#cite:103) while schedule rates move only through a clause allowing three increases a period inside a window with approval beyond 10% [117](#cite:117); GSA itself suspended those limits in 2022 when inflation outran them [117](#cite:117). Using recruiting and retention evidence in rate discussions is practice guidance; the market series and CALC+ comparables are the documented evidence [103](#cite:103) [111](#cite:111). The trade-off (relief unavailable or too slow for the vacancy) is consistent with the mechanism.
queries: GSAR 552.216-70 economic price adjustment
BLS ECI June 2026

original.challenge: Larger employers offer stronger total compensation
original.mitigation: Explain the full package and genuine small-company advantages in role scope, access, flexibility, and growth.
original.tradeoff: Noncash advantages will not offset every material pay gap.
original.dependencies: Requires credible career paths (G2), workable schedules (G6), and sustainable pay (D1).

entries.evidence: Larger employers total compensation is larger on the benefits line (97% vs 59% offer coverage; family premium \$26,993) [105](#cite:105) and benefits are 30% of cost [104](#cite:104); the rows "genuine advantages in role scope, access, flexibility and growth" are real compensation by the amenity evidence (WFH 8%, schedule predictability 20% of wages) [115](#cite:115) [94](#cite:94); "noncash advantages will not offset every material pay gap" is consistent with job and organisation characteristics predicting choice [63](#cite:63). Whether explaining the package changes acceptance has not been tested directly (synthesis).
queries: Mas Pallais 2017 valuing alternative work arrangements
KFF 2025 employer health benefits
BLS ECEC June 2026

original.challenge: New-hire pay creates internal inequity
original.mitigation: Review comparable incumbents when setting offers; budget necessary adjustments.
original.tradeoff: One hire can trigger multiple incumbent raises.
original.dependencies: Links directly to offer affordability (D1), retention reviews (G1), and rate relief (D2).

entries.evidence: External hires into comparable jobs started about 18% above internal promotees and performed worse for two years [93](#cite:93); employees who learn peers pay react asymmetrically, with below-median earners searching more [92](#cite:92); the Equal Pay Act requires curing gaps upward [112](#cite:112); right-to-discuss laws lower wages ~2% as employers avoid renegotiation [90](#cite:90). "One hire can trigger multiple incumbent raises" and the links to D1, G1 and D2 follow.
queries: Bidwell 2011 paying more to get less
Card Mas Moretti Saez 2012 peer salaries
Cullen Pakzad-Hurson 2023

original.challenge: Fees, relocation and bonuses erode margin
original.mitigation: Set an all-in acquisition budget per role, considering expected vacancy duration.
original.tradeoff: Tight limits prolong vacancies; generous spending may not be recovered.
original.dependencies: Requires vacancy cost (D7), source performance (H8), and expected retention (G1).

entries.evidence: The components the row names are priced in the benchmark: median cost-per-hire \$1,200 nonexecutive and \$10,625 executive in 2025 with agency fees, relocation and bonuses among the components [196](#cite:196); sign-on bonuses are used by 80 percent of organisations and evaluated by 12 percent [118](#cite:118), and on cost-type work are allowable only under a plan that predates the work [100](#cite:100). The mitigation, an all-in acquisition budget per role set against expected vacancy duration, is consistent with the cost evidence and unstudied; the trade-off, tight limits prolong vacancies and generous spending may not be recovered, follows from the retention evidence. Dependencies on D7 and H8 are adjudicated here, G1 in sweep 6.
queries: SHRM 2025 recruiting benchmarking report cost per hire

original.challenge: Nonbillable payroll and payment timing strain cash
original.mitigation: Cap hiring-ahead exposure; stage developmental hires against credible demand.
original.tradeoff: Lower cash exposure can slow response when work becomes available.
original.dependencies: Constrains bridge work (C4), training cohorts (F8), and workforce forecasting (H1).

entries.evidence: The timing gap is a rule: a proper invoice is paid in 30 days by default [202](#cite:202) with a 15-day goal for small business contractors [201](#cite:201), payroll before billing is indirect cost [148](#cite:148), and a clearance cannot be requested ahead of a need [119](#cite:119). The mitigation, cap hiring-ahead exposure and stage developmental hires against credible demand, follows from those rules and is unstudied; the trade-off, slower response when work arrives, is stated. The dependencies on C4, F8 and H1 are links (k-132, k-137).
queries: Prompt Payment Act 5 CFR 1315.4; FAR 32.009-1 accelerated payments

original.challenge: Vacancy cost is invisible while recruiting spend is visible
original.mitigation: Estimate foregone contribution, delivery disruption, and management burden alongside recruiting spend.
original.tradeoff: Estimates need assumptions; unbilled revenue is not equivalent to lost profit.
original.dependencies: Requires credible openings (H2), workload evidence (G5), and vacancy priority (H3).

entries.evidence: Vacancy cost is measurable and measured: about a fifth of salary per replacement in the case-study median, with the indirect costs mostly left out of the studies [180](#cite:180); unit turnover lowers customer satisfaction and productivity at about −.22 and profit margin at −.15 [181](#cite:181); on a T&M contract the vacancy is unbilled hours [99](#cite:99). The mitigation, estimate foregone contribution, delivery disruption and management burden alongside recruiting spend, is the cost-benefit method those sources apply; the trade-off, that estimates need assumptions and unbilled revenue is not lost profit, is the caveat the review itself states [180](#cite:180). Dependencies on H2, G5 and H3 are adjudicated.
queries: Boushey Glynn 2012 cost of turnover; Heavey 2013 unit performance

original.challenge: No single owner from opening to start
original.mitigation: Assign one accountable owner and responsibilities for screening, customer coordination, and offers.
original.tradeoff: Owner needs protected time and decision authority.
original.dependencies: Enables faster decisions (E2), customer follow-through (E5), and onboarding (C6).

entries.evidence: No study of single-owner requisition management was found. The consequences the row points at are measured, earlier offers accepted more often [15](#cite:15), withdrawal after a badly perceived process [16](#cite:16), and 22 percent higher no-show odds per week between acceptance and start [144](#cite:144), and small organisations run six requisitions per recruiter [196](#cite:196); whether one accountable owner shortens those clocks is synthesis. The mitigation and its trade-off (protected time and authority) are carried as such.
queries: requisition owner accountability time to fill (no evidence surfaced)

original.challenge: Slow scheduling and approvals lose candidates
original.mitigation: Reserve interview windows; set response targets and offer approval ranges.
original.tradeoff: Requires disciplined availability from busy managers.
original.dependencies: Requires ownership (E1), preapproved pay (D1), and customer review commitments (E5).

entries.evidence: Mechanism supported: earlier post-interview offers were more likely to be accepted with no performance or turnover penalty (N = 3,012) [15](#cite:15); process perceptions predict acceptance intentions [14](#cite:14); 41% of organisations report rising ghosting [43](#cite:43). The specific mitigations (reserved windows, response targets, pre-approved ranges) are practice guidance not tested as such; "customer review commitments" is deferred to sweep 7.
queries: Becker Connolly Slaughter 2010 job offer timing

original.challenge: Screening overweights keywords or exact program history
original.mitigation: Use consistent job-related questions and a brief practical assessment of transferable skills.
original.tradeoff: Requires technical time; assessment should be proportionate.
original.dependencies: Depends on scorecard (B5) and valid requirements (B2); expands adjacent sourcing (A2).

entries.evidence: Keyword and exact-match screens reject qualified candidates (88% of employers) [44](#cite:44) and the proxies they use are weak (years of experience .07) [1](#cite:1); consistent job-related questions and practical assessment are the most valid predictors (structured interview .42, job knowledge .40, work sample .33) [1](#cite:1); mechanical combination beats judgement (.44 vs .28) [7](#cite:7). The trade-off as stated (technical time; proportionate assessment) is consistent with the evidence summaries [17](#cite:17).
queries: Sackett 2022 validity
Hidden Workers ATS 88%
Kuncel 2013 mechanical vs clinical

original.challenge: Long or repetitive interviews cause withdrawal
original.mitigation: Combine overlapping interviews; explain the process at first contact.
original.tradeoff: Fewer interviews increase the importance of selecting useful questions.
original.dependencies: Requires shared criteria (B5), disciplined assessment (E3), and scheduling (E2).

entries.evidence: Withdrawal tracks perceptions of the process and differs by stage [16](#cite:16); procedural-justice and face-validity perceptions predict acceptance intentions [14](#cite:14); developers name time demands and anxiety as reasons to avoid technical interviews [22](#cite:22). No primary study of the number of interview rounds against withdrawal was found (the query returned vendor blogs only), so "long or repetitive interviews cause withdrawal" is supported in mechanism, not in magnitude. The stated trade-off (fewer interviews raise the stakes of each question) is a synthesis.
queries: Ryan Sacco McFarland Kriska 2000 withdrawal
number of interview rounds candidate drop-off survey 2024 2025 (vendor blogs only)

original.challenge: Customer approval stalls after internal review
original.mitigation: Agree on review milestones and escalation contacts.
original.tradeoff: The company cannot unilaterally control the customer decision cycle.
original.dependencies: Requires credible opening (H2), feedback criteria (B6), and vacancy owner (E1).

entries.evidence: No study of customer approval cycles for contractor staff was found. The structure is in the rules: the clause carried gives the contractor 30 days to propose a substitute and the government no period to answer [188](#cite:188), and the personal-services rule leaves the decision with the customer [197](#cite:197); the consequence is in the speed and withdrawal evidence [15](#cite:15) [16](#cite:16). The mitigation, agree review milestones and escalation contacts, is carried as a lever without evidence of effect; the trade-off, no unilateral control of the customer's cycle, is the condition.
queries: customer approval of contractor personnel turnaround (no evidence surfaced)

original.challenge: Basic expectations surface too late
original.mitigation: Discuss salary, onsite attendance, duties, clearance, and timing early.
original.tradeoff: Candor may reduce pipeline size but exposes real mismatches sooner.
original.dependencies: Requires pay range (D1), defined duties (B1), access facts (C3), and schedule limits (G6).

entries.evidence: Surfacing hard facts early is the realistic job preview, which lowers inflated expectations and attrition during recruiting and reduces turnover [12](#cite:12), mainly through perceived honesty [13](#cite:13). Qualified: the law fixes when some facts may be asked for, not told: disability-related questions wait for a conditional offer [34](#cite:34), criminal history for contract positions likewise [48](#cite:48), and citizenship may not be a posting restriction for export-controlled work [49](#cite:49). Salary discussion timing is constrained by state salary-history bans (sweep 3).
queries: Phillips 1998 RJP meta-analysis
Earnest Allen Landis 2011

original.challenge: Accepted candidates withdraw or take counteroffers
original.mitigation: Maintain contact through start; confirm motivations and retain viable backups.
original.tradeoff: Extra effort cannot eliminate competing offers.
original.dependencies: Depends on total value (D3), timely access (C6), and maintained pipeline (E8).

entries.evidence: Maintaining contact and speed are supported in mechanism: earlier offers are accepted more often with no later penalty [15](#cite:15), and process perceptions predict acceptance intentions [14](#cite:14). Counteroffers themselves rest only on a staffing firms survey (58% of managers counter; mean stay 1.7 years after accepting) [113](#cite:113); no peer-reviewed study was found. "Retain viable backups" is untested as a practice.
queries: counteroffer acceptance evidence study
Becker 2010 offer timing

original.challenge: Candidate records are scattered or discarded
original.mitigation: Keep a shared pipeline with reasons, next actions, and permission-based follow-up.
original.tradeoff: Needs data hygiene and appropriate handling of candidate information.
original.dependencies: Requires ownership (E1); supports passive outreach (A3) and diagnosis (H8).

entries.evidence: Most of the record the row asks for is required by law: application and selection records for a year from the decision and until disposition of any charge [200](#cite:200), applicant-flow records by group for the adverse-impact computation [31](#cite:31), four years under California's automated-decision rules [40](#cite:40); the contractor-specific Internet Applicant duty goes with the EO 11246 regulations on October 26, 2026 [86](#cite:86). The mitigation, a shared pipeline with reasons, next actions and permission-based follow-up, is the record those rules require plus the stage-and-reason field the evidence review needs [204](#cite:204); the trade-off, data hygiene and appropriate handling, is the retention and privacy rule itself.
queries: 29 CFR 1602.14 record retention; UGESP 1607.4 records

original.challenge: Strong fundamentals but insufficient domain experience
original.mitigation: Create a bounded learning plan with measurable readiness milestones.
original.tradeoff: Training takes time and does not guarantee customer acceptance.
original.dependencies: Requires acceptance path (B4), relevant exercises (F3), and identified placement (F6).

entries.evidence: The challenge is supported in mechanism: output rose 53 percent over the first year where it could be counted, with pay much flatter [157](#cite:157), and task mastery correlates .38 with performance [152](#cite:152); the rate assumes the finished worker [98](#cite:98). The mitigation, a bounded learning plan with measurable readiness milestones, is consistent with the transfer evidence that realistic tasks and early use matter [162](#cite:162), but no study of milestone plans themselves was found. The trade-off, that training does not guarantee customer acceptance, is supported by the labor-category rule and its enforcement [99](#cite:99) [173](#cite:173). Dependencies on B4 wait for sweep 7.
queries: Shaw Lazear 2008 tenure and output; Bauer 2025 task mastery

original.challenge: Senior employees lack mentoring capacity
original.mitigation: Allocate mentoring time explicitly; limit concurrent trainees.
original.tradeoff: Reduces senior delivery capacity in the short term.
original.dependencies: Requires workload relief (G5), funded cohort capacity (F8), and customer ramp agreement (B4).

entries.evidence: The challenge is supported: learning from knowledgeable coworkers is 4 to 9 percent of compensation [158](#cite:158), the social tactics that put insiders beside newcomers are the strongest onboarding predictors [152](#cite:152), and on a T&M contract the hours come from billable seniors or go into the indirect pools [99](#cite:99) [148](#cite:148) [175](#cite:175). The mitigation, allocate mentoring time explicitly and limit concurrent trainees, follows from the cost rules but has no study behind it; the measurable gains to the protégé are small [164](#cite:164) [165](#cite:165). The trade-off, reduced senior delivery capacity, is the mechanism itself. Dependencies on G5 and B4 wait for sweeps 6 and 7.
queries: Jarosch Oberfield Rossi-Hansberg learning from coworkers; Allen 2004 mentoring meta-analysis; Eby 2008

original.challenge: Training does not reflect actual work
original.mitigation: Use sanitized representative tasks and customer-approved competencies.
original.tradeoff: Preparation takes effort; actual program material may be unavailable.
original.dependencies: Requires clear deliverables (B1), mentoring (F2), and a readiness plan (F1).

entries.evidence: Transfer depends on realistic training environments, behavioural modelling, error management, supervisor support (ρ .31 against .14 for peers), transfer climate (.37) and an early opportunity to perform [162](#cite:162), with motivation and self-efficacy mattering most for open skills [163](#cite:163). The mitigation, sanitized representative tasks and customer-approved competencies, is the realistic-environment condition applied to classified work; the trade-off, that the actual material may be unavailable, is stated as synthesis. The coefficients are carried from a peer-reviewed review; the Blume meta-analysis is a todo.
queries: Blume Ford Baldwin Huang 2010 transfer of training meta-analysis; Grossman Salas 2011

original.challenge: Customer will not accept junior personnel
original.mitigation: Explore a defined junior work package, supervised role, or approved staffing mix.
original.tradeoff: May require task, labor-category, or pricing changes.
original.dependencies: Requires eligibility review (B3), work-model approval (H7), and mentoring capacity (F2).

entries.evidence: Labor-category qualifications are a contract term: hours by people who do not meet them are not paid [99](#cite:99) [98](#cite:98), and an Inspector General found 101 of 112 unqualified employees improperly charged with about \$35 million in potential improper payments [173](#cite:173); a cyber role needs its certificate on commencement [139](#cite:139). The mitigation, a defined junior work package, supervised role or approved staffing mix, is the rule's own remedy, billing each person at the category they meet; the trade-off, that it may require task, labor-category or pricing changes, follows. The by-name customer approval mechanics (B3, H7) wait for sweep 7.
queries: DoD IG labor category qualifications audit OASIS DODIG-2019-029

original.challenge: Employees leave after gaining skills or clearance
original.mitigation: Plan compensation and career reviews at readiness milestones; identify the next assignment.
original.tradeoff: Retention costs rise as external market value grows.
original.dependencies: Requires pay progression (G1), career options (G2), and cohort economics (F7).

entries.evidence: The challenge is supported: general skills are portable, firms pay for them because of an informational advantage [161](#cite:161) and keep the productivity–wage wedge only while the person stays [159](#cite:159); the cleared market pays a premium and 13 percent switched employers for pay in a year [89](#cite:89). The mitigation, compensation and career reviews at readiness milestones, is a retain-stage question (G1, G2; sweep 6) and untested here; what sweep 5 adds is that paying for education retains mostly by sorting [160](#cite:160) and that repayment terms, which cut quitting about 15 percent in cited research [166](#cite:166), are now barred or narrowed in California and Colorado [167](#cite:167) [168](#cite:168). The trade-off, that retention costs rise with external market value, is the mechanism.
queries: Manchester 2012 tuition reimbursement retention sorting; CFPB employer-driven debt 2023; California AB 692

original.challenge: Training begins without a credible placement
original.mitigation: Tie developmental investment to forecast demand and a specific acceptance path.
original.tradeoff: Reduces speculative exposure but can limit pipeline depth.
original.dependencies: Requires confirmed demand (H2), forecast (H1), and customer acceptance (F4).

entries.evidence: The rules bound speculative development: training for non-employees is unallowable [175](#cite:175), a clearance cannot be requested ahead of a need [119](#cite:119), SkillBridge owes offers to 75 percent of completers [74](#cite:74), and apprenticeship brings registration and reporting that smaller employers find hard [172](#cite:172). The mitigation, tie the investment to forecast demand and a specific acceptance path, is consistent with all of them and has no effectiveness evidence; whether the demand is real is H1/H2, sweep 7. The trade-off, less speculative exposure for less pipeline depth, is synthesis.
queries: FAR 31.205-44 training costs; GAO-25-107040 apprenticeship

original.challenge: Any departure is treated as proof development failed
original.mitigation: Assess cohort investment, productive service, and contribution before departure.
original.tradeoff: Requires tracking over time; some individual investments will fail.
original.dependencies: Requires training costs (F8), retention evidence (G1), and consistent records (H8).

entries.evidence: The challenge, that any departure is read as proof development failed, is supported by omission: the federal cost-benefit study of apprenticeship measured participants and society and nothing on the employer's side [171](#cite:171), and no study of employer returns to in-house development at small firms was found. The mitigation, assess cohort investment, productive service and contribution, is the method the economics imply, cost against output over tenure [159](#cite:159) [157](#cite:157), stated as synthesis; the trade-off, tracking over time with some individual failures, follows.
queries: Reed 2012 apprenticeship cost-benefit; Dearden Reed Van Reenen 2006

original.challenge: Development funding is too small or inconsistent
original.mitigation: Fund a bounded pilot with capacity limits and stop or continue criteria.
original.tradeoff: Small pilots yield limited volume and take time to evaluate.
original.dependencies: Requires cash capacity (D6), mentors (F2), and a recovery measure (F7).

entries.evidence: Cost and inconsistency of funding are among the barriers GAO records from employers, with smaller employers naming registration and reporting burden [172](#cite:172); the tax code's \$5,250 exclusion [174](#cite:174) and the allowability of job-related training in the rates [175](#cite:175) are the funding channels. The mitigation, a bounded pilot with capacity limits and stop or continue criteria, is unstudied; its trade-off, limited volume and slow evaluation, follows from the two-year horizon of any cohort measure (synthesis). The dependency on D6 (cash) waits for sweep 7.
queries: IRS section 127 FS-2026-10; GAO apprenticeship employer barriers

original.challenge: Pay lags employee capability
original.mitigation: Review compensation proactively against responsibilities and market evidence.
original.tradeoff: Recurring cost may require customer rate discussions.
original.dependencies: Requires rate feasibility (D2), internal equity (D4), and readiness milestones (F5).

entries.evidence: Pay predicts quitting modestly (ρ −.17) and the alternatives a person sees more (.23) [178](#cite:178); quits at a large employer responded to peers' pay more than to the market and were insensitive when raises were similar [182](#cite:182); below-median earners who learn peer pay search [92](#cite:92); external hires start 18 percent above promotees [93](#cite:93); cleared professionals switch for pay [89](#cite:89). The mitigation, review compensation proactively against responsibilities and market evidence, is consistent with the comparison mechanism if the review keeps peers level [182](#cite:182) [112](#cite:112); no study of proactive pay review itself was found. The trade-off, recurring cost and customer rate discussions, is the rate ceiling [98](#cite:98). Dependencies on D2 and D4 are now links (k-095, k-097); F5 is adjudicated.
queries: Rubenstein 2018 turnover meta-analysis; Dube Giuliano Leonard 2019 fairness and frictions

original.challenge: Small-company promotion paths are limited
original.mitigation: Define meaningful technical growth, mentoring, leadership, and cross-program options.
original.tradeoff: Titles alone will not substitute for meaningful work or compensation.
original.dependencies: Requires actual demand (H1), transfer planning (H4), and sustainable pay (D1).

entries.evidence: Internal mobility is among the practices most strongly tied to lower unit turnover (ρ −.25) [181](#cite:181), which supports the challenge; the promotion a small firm can offer is the one the evidence warns about, since firms promote on current output and the teams under those managers do 7.5 percent worse per doubling of the manager's prior sales [184](#cite:184) [185](#cite:185). The mitigation, meaningful technical growth, mentoring, leadership and cross-program options, is consistent with both findings and unstudied as a package; the trade-off, that titles do not substitute for work or pay, follows from pay's own predictor (−.17) and from the work-related predictors [178](#cite:178). Dependencies on H1 and H4 wait for sweep 7 (H4 adjudicated here).
queries: Heavey Holwerda Hausknecht 2013 collective turnover; Benson Li Shue Peter Principle

original.challenge: Employees feel disconnected from the company
original.mitigation: Use useful manager check-ins, recognition, and career conversations.
original.tradeoff: Management time is needed; avoid meetings without employee value.
original.dependencies: Supports career planning (G2) and early detection of work problems (G4).

entries.evidence: Commitment (−.29), fit (−.29), embeddedness (−.26) and leadership (−.24) are the cluster of predictors after wanting to leave [178](#cite:178); unit engagement relates to turnover across 7,939 business units [183](#cite:183). The mitigation, useful manager check-ins, recognition and career conversations, stands on those correlations and on the harm an undermining supervisor does (HR 3.01) [156](#cite:156); recognition programs and stay interviews as such have no evidence found. The trade-off, management time and meetings without value, is stated as synthesis. G3 and G4 are merged into one constraint because the predictors do not separate them.
queries: Harter Schmidt Hayes 2002 business-unit engagement meta-analysis

original.challenge: Work is frustrating, stagnant or poorly managed
original.mitigation: Use stay interviews; address workload, supervision, tools, and fit with the customer.
original.tradeoff: The company may have limited control over the work environment.
original.dependencies: Requires customer engagement (B1), workload evidence (G5), and alternatives (H4).

entries.evidence: Satisfaction (−.28), leadership (−.24), fit (−.29) and stress (.21) predict quitting [178](#cite:178), and the supervisor's conduct in the first ninety days predicts leaving [156](#cite:156); the challenge is supported. The mitigation names stay interviews, which have no evidence base found, and addressing workload, supervision, tools and fit, which is what the predictors point at; the trade-off, limited control over a customer-run work environment, is the condition of the pack and is stated as synthesis. Dependencies on B1 wait for sweep 7; G5 and H4 are adjudicated here.
queries: Rubenstein 2018 leadership satisfaction stress predictors

original.challenge: Vacancies overload staff and trigger more exits
original.mitigation: Show capacity risks; negotiate priorities and temporary support.
original.tradeoff: Customer may need to accept reduced scope or slower delivery.
original.dependencies: Requires vacancy prioritization (H3), partner options (H6), and mentoring limits (F2).

entries.evidence: The mechanism is supported through strain rather than hours: stress and exhaustion (.21), role conflict (.15) and work–life conflict (.19) predict quitting while workload as such is −.10 [178](#cite:178) and staffing levels are not significantly related to unit turnover [181](#cite:181). The mitigation, show capacity risks and negotiate priorities or temporary support, is consistent with the key-personnel clause's notice and substitute mechanics [188](#cite:188) and unstudied as practice; the trade-off, reduced scope or slower delivery, follows. Dependencies on H3 and H6 wait for sweep 7; F2 is adjudicated.
queries: Rubenstein 2018 workload stress role conflict; Heavey 2013 staffing levels

original.challenge: Onsite schedules and commuting reduce appeal
original.mitigation: Seek approved scheduling flexibility; explain restrictions accurately.
original.tradeoff: Classified or operational needs may limit flexibility.
original.dependencies: Requires customer requirement review (B2); affects geographic sourcing (A1) and offers (E6).

entries.evidence: Workers price a work-from-home option at about 8 percent of wages and schedule predictability at about 20 percent [115](#cite:115), working conditions are compensation in their own right [94](#cite:94), and a commute of 45 minutes or more raised transfer probability ten points among teachers [194](#cite:194). The mitigation, seek approved flexibility and explain restrictions accurately, matches the amenity evidence and the honesty mechanism of realistic previews [13](#cite:13); the trade-off, that classified or operational needs limit flexibility, is the facility rule [119](#cite:119). Dependencies on B2 wait for sweep 7; the links to A1 and E6 are drawn (k-105).
queries: Mas Pallais 2017 valuing alternative work arrangements; commuting distance turnover study

original.challenge: Employees fear contract discontinuity
original.mitigation: Communicate known facts, maintain redeployment options, and explain uncertainty honestly.
original.tradeoff: The company cannot promise assignments it does not control.
original.dependencies: Requires demand visibility (H1), confirmed work (H2), and transfer planning (H4).

entries.evidence: Wanting to leave (.56) and perceived alternatives (.23) are the strongest predictors [178](#cite:178), and a contract's visible end supplies both; the right of first refusal with a successor contractor was revoked in January 2025 and its rule rescinded in December 2025 [186](#cite:186), so the firm cannot point to it. The mitigation, communicate known facts, maintain redeployment options and explain uncertainty honestly, rests on the honesty mechanism by which realistic previews lower turnover [13](#cite:13); no study of contract-end communication among contractor staff was found. The trade-off, that the company cannot promise assignments it does not control, is the condition. Dependencies on H1, H2 and H4 wait for sweep 7 (H4 adjudicated here).
queries: EO 14055 nondisplacement revoked 29 CFR part 9 rescinded

original.challenge: Prime or another employer hires away successful staff
original.mitigation: Strengthen reasons to stay; maintain succession options and professional transitions.
original.tradeoff: Some mobility is unavoidable; retention cannot rely solely on restrictions.
original.dependencies: Requires competitive value (D3), career paths (G2), and knowledge coverage (H5).

entries.evidence: External hires are paid about 18 percent more than internal promotees [93](#cite:93) and 13 percent of cleared professionals switched employers for pay in a year [89](#cite:89), which supports the challenge; the firm may not agree with the prime not to hire each other's people, and a non-solicit term survives only as a collateral part of a real collaboration [187](#cite:187), which supports the row's own trade-off that retention cannot rely on restrictions. The mitigation, strengthen reasons to stay and maintain succession, maps onto embeddedness (−.26) [178](#cite:178) and firm-specific training (−.40) [181](#cite:181) and onto the handover levers; untested as a package. Dependencies on D3 are adjudicated; G2 and H5 here.
queries: DOJ FTC antitrust guidelines business activities affecting workers 2025; Bidwell external premium

original.challenge: Recruiting starts only after urgency arises
original.mitigation: Maintain a rolling demand forecast and relationships for recurring skills.
original.tradeoff: Forecasts can be wrong; pipelines require effort without an immediate opening.
original.dependencies: Requires customer demand confidence (H2), candidate records (E8), and cash limits (D6).

entries.evidence: The cost of starting at the vacancy is measurable in the clocks: a 45-day median fill [43](#cite:43) and a 197-to-243-day clearance [126](#cite:126) from a standing start, against 87 percent of small firms reporting few qualified applicants [71](#cite:71). The mitigation, a rolling demand forecast and relationships for recurring skills, is the government's own planning guidance [205](#cite:205) and the pipeline evidence [60](#cite:60) [74](#cite:74); no study of forecast accuracy at small contractors was found, and a cache of cleared people cannot be built [119](#cite:119). The trade-off, that forecasts can be wrong and pipelines cost effort, is stated. Dependencies on H2, E8 and D6 are adjudicated.
queries: GAO-04-39 strategic workforce planning principles

original.challenge: Openings are tentative, unfunded or weakly sponsored
original.mitigation: Confirm funding, decision authority, start date, and intent before substantial recruiting spend.
original.tradeoff: May delay sourcing for work that later becomes real.
original.dependencies: Requires customer milestones (E5); governs training (F6) and vacancy valuation (D7).

entries.evidence: The rules make a tentative opening expensive: a clearance may be requested only for a contract need and never to build a cache, and a pre-employment investigation needs a written commitment and a start within 45 days [119](#cite:119); a proposed key person must be reported if unavailable [108](#cite:108) and may not be named without a reasonable basis to deliver them, on pain of the award being unwound [203](#cite:203); accepted hires disappear with every week of waiting [144](#cite:144). The mitigation, confirm funding, decision authority, start date and intent before substantial recruiting spend, is the logic of those rules; the trade-off, delayed sourcing for work that later becomes real, follows. The dependency on E5 is adjudicated here, F6 in sweep 5 and D7 here.
queries: GAO B-421008 ASRC bait and switch key personnel; 32 CFR 117.10(a)(5)

original.challenge: Every vacancy gets equal priority
original.mitigation: Rank delivery impact, customer importance, economic value, and feasibility.
original.tradeoff: Some openings receive less attention; leaders must accept that choice.
original.dependencies: Requires vacancy economics (D7), workload risk (G5), and opening credibility (H2).

entries.evidence: Vacancies can be ranked because their cost can be estimated: replacement cost by salary share [180](#cite:180), unit-level effects on customers and productivity [181](#cite:181), the strain on those covering [178](#cite:178), and unbilled hours [99](#cite:99). The mitigation, rank delivery impact, customer importance, economic value and feasibility, is consistent with those measures and unstudied as a practice; the trade-off, that some openings get less attention and leaders must own the choice, is stated. Dependencies on D7, G5 and H2 are adjudicated.

original.challenge: Internal moves create a new vacancy elsewhere
original.mitigation: Assess net company impact and sequence backfills.
original.tradeoff: A move helping one program may damage another relationship.
original.dependencies: Requires demand forecast (H1), priorities (H3), and succession coverage (H5).

entries.evidence: Internal mobility is among the practices most tied to lower unit turnover (−.25) [181](#cite:181), so the move keeps the person; the vacancy it leaves carries the full posting-to-clearance clock [126](#cite:126) and, for a named key person, the customer's consent and an equal-or-better substitute [188](#cite:188). The mitigation, assess net company impact and sequence backfills, follows from those rules and is unstudied; the trade-off, one program helped and another's relationship damaged, is synthesis. Dependencies on H1 and H3 wait for sweep 7; H5 is adjudicated here.
queries: Heavey 2013 internal mobility; HHSAR key personnel clause

original.challenge: Essential knowledge sits with a few people
original.mitigation: Cross-train, document handoffs, and build succession coverage.
original.tradeoff: Uses current delivery time to reduce future disruption.
original.dependencies: Requires mentor capacity (F2) and workload relief (G5); reduces departure impact (G8).

entries.evidence: When a worker dies unexpectedly, the firm raises the remaining same-occupation workers' pay to keep them, other occupations lose value, and replacement costs are largest for specialised skills in thin markets [193](#cite:193); unit turnover lowers customer satisfaction and productivity at about −.22 [181](#cite:181). The mitigation, cross-train, document handoffs and build succession coverage, is supported in its first part by firm-specific training's −.40 with unit turnover [181](#cite:181) and by the substitute requirement of key-personnel clauses [188](#cite:188), and the succession metrics are in the human-capital standard [46](#cite:46); documentation itself is unstudied. The trade-off, current delivery time, is the senior-hours cost (k-114). Dependencies on F2 and G5 are adjudicated.
queries: Jäger Heining how substitutable are workers; ISO 30414 succession

original.challenge: Partner support has unclear approval or economics
original.mitigation: Explore customer-approved teaming or subcontract support for specific gaps.
original.tradeoff: Lower margin, reduced control, and contractual approval needs.
original.dependencies: Requires customer requirements (B2), affordable rates (D1), and vacancy impact (D7).

entries.evidence: The approval and the economics the row calls unclear are specified: advance consent for cost-type, T&M and labor-hour subcontracts without an approved purchasing system [199](#cite:199); no more than half the amount paid on a set-aside services contract to non-similarly-situated subcontractors [198](#cite:198); subcontractor labor at its own category rates [98](#cite:98); no agreement with the partner not to hire each other's people [187](#cite:187). The mitigation, customer-approved teaming or subcontract support for specific gaps, is the rules' own path; the trade-off, lower margin, reduced control and approvals, is in the rules. Dependencies on B2, D1 and D7 are adjudicated.
queries: FAR 52.219-14 limitations on subcontracting; FAR 52.244-2 consent

original.challenge: Some roles are structurally hard to staff profitably
original.mitigation: Consider approved work redistribution, team delivery, or rate and scope changes.
original.tradeoff: Existing contract terms may prevent the preferred change.
original.dependencies: Requires clear duties (B1), category eligibility (B3), and rate analysis (D2).

entries.evidence: The mechanism is arithmetic from the rules: a billing rate is built from fringe, overhead, G&A and profit [206](#cite:206) under a category rate fixed at award [98](#cite:98) and schedule ceilings [111](#cite:111), against market pay [110](#cite:110) rising about 3 percent a year [103](#cite:103) with at most three adjustments a period [117](#cite:117); no source states the feasibility test as such and the pack marks it synthesis. The mitigation, approved work redistribution, team delivery, or rate and scope changes, follows from the category and adjustment rules; the trade-off, that existing terms may bar the preferred change, is the adjustment clause's own limits. Dependencies on B1, B3 and D2 are adjudicated.
queries: DOT SBIR cost proposal instructions indirect rates; GSA CALC+ ceilings

original.challenge: Discussion relies on anecdotes instead of evidence
original.mitigation: Track where candidates stop progressing and record specific reasons.
original.tradeoff: Needs consistent definitions; avoid burdensome reporting.
original.dependencies: Requires pipeline records (E8), common scorecard (B5), and accountable ownership (E1).

entries.evidence: Nearly a thousand HR professionals disagreed with the selection research on the predictors that matter most [204](#cite:204), which supports the challenge; the records that would correct anecdote are largely required by law [200](#cite:200) [31](#cite:31) [40](#cite:40) and named by the human-capital standard [46](#cite:46). The mitigation, track where candidates stop progressing and record specific reasons, is the record plus a stage-and-reason field; the trade-off, consistent definitions without burdensome reporting, is the standard's own caveat. Dependencies on E8, B5 and E1 are adjudicated.
queries: Rynes Colbert Brown 2002 HR beliefs research practice gap
